title: Surface-condition-mediated supercooling of the A-B transition in confined superfluid helium-3
authors: Daksh Malhotra, Aymar Muhikira, Alexander J. Shook, John P. Davis
abstract: Chiral $p$-wave superconductors and superfluids are central model systems in the search for topological quantum matter, but in reduced dimensions their properties are inseparable from the boundary conditions imposed by surrounding surfaces. Superfluid $^3$He provides a uniquely clean, well-established spin-triplet $p$-wave condensate in which these boundary conditions can be engineered directly. Here, we use a fourth-sound Helmholtz resonator to study the A--B phase transition of $^3$He confined to a $1.8\,μ$m cavity after preplating the internal surfaces with $\sim4$ atomic layers of $^4$He. In contrast to our previous fourth-sound measurements, which showed no resolvable hysteresis in the transition temperature, the preplated device exhibits a clear separation between cooling and warming transition temperatures together with stochastic run-to-run variations. The hysteresis decreases toward the highest pressures studied, consistent with previous observations of the pressure dependence of $^4$He-mediated quasiparticle boundary scattering. These results demonstrate that surface preparation can qualitatively modify first-order transition kinetics in confined $^3$He, making boundary conditions an experimentally accessible control parameter for metastability and for future studies of reduced-dimension topological superfluid states.
summary: This research uses a confined superfluid $	ext{He}^3$ resonator to study the first-order A–B phase transition. By preplating the internal surfaces with $	ext{}^4	ext{He}$, the authors induced a measurable thermal hysteresis, proving that surface boundary conditions can qualitatively control the transition kinetics. This establishes surface preparation as a key experimental knob for controlling metastability in topological superfluid systems.
main_problem: The study investigates how surface boundary conditions qualitatively modify the kinetics of the first-order A–B phase transition in confined superfluid Helium-3.
main_result: Preplating the internal surfaces with $	ext{}^4	ext{He}$ causes the appearance of a clear cooling-warming hysteresis in the transition temperature, demonstrating that surface preparation acts as a controllable parameter for metastability.
method: The experiment uses a fourth-sound Helmholtz resonator to measure the superfluid fraction during controlled cooling and warming sweeps, comparing results with and without surface preplating.
model_or_system: The system is superfluid $	ext{He}^3$ confined to a $1.8\ \mu	ext{m}$ cavity. The A-B transition is a first-order phase transition whose kinetics are sensitive to boundary conditions imposed by the surrounding surfaces.
key_observables: Thermal hysteresis ($\Delta T_{	ext{hyst}}$) between cooling and warming transition temperatures, and the mode frequency shift tracking the superfluid fraction.
important_parameters: Confinement size ($1.8\ \mu	ext{m}$), surface preplating layer ($\sim 4$ atomic layers of $	ext{}^4	ext{He}$), and applied pressure ($P$).
main_assumptions: The observed hysteresis is attributed to kinetic barriers controlled by the surface state, which is consistent with theoretical models of boundary scattering.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the resonator setup, temperature sweeps showing the A $\leftrightarrow$ B switching signature, and plots comparing measured hysteresis dependence on pressure against Ginzburg-Landau predictions for different scattering types.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical system and the problem of surface influence, presents experimental measurements comparing preplated vs. non-preplated samples, analyzes the resulting hysteresis and its pressure dependence, and concludes by linking these findings to boundary-controlled kinetics.
why_interesting: This work provides a clean, tunable platform to study non-equilibrium phase transitions in a quantum fluid, directly linking macroscopic thermodynamic measurements (hysteresis) to microscopic boundary physics, which is highly relevant for understanding topological states in reduced dimensions.
